Lecture 6

Diagonalization, Cayley–Hamilton, Functions of Operators

By the end of this lecture you will be able to

Problems · 21 Present Notes (PDF) Problem sheet (PDF)

In Lecture 5 we found the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of an operator. We saw that, with enough linearly independent eigenvectors, the matrix of the operator becomes diagonal. In this lecture we state exactly when an operator is diagonalizable. We prove the Cayley–Hamilton theorem: every operator satisfies its own characteristic equation. Then we use diagonalization to compute functions of operators. The most important of them is the exponential etAe^{tA}etA. It solves linear differential equations, and in the form e−iH^t/ℏe^{-i\hat Ht/\hbar}e−iH^t/ℏ it describes time evolution in quantum mechanics.

The main idea is simple. In an eigenbasis the operator only multiplies each basis vector by its eigenvalue. So everything we do with numbers (raise to a power, compute an exponential, apply a function) we can also do with the operator: separately for each eigenvalue.

Diagonalizable operators

Definition 6.1 (Diagonalizable operator). An operator T∈L(V)T\in\Lin(V)T∈L(V) is called diagonalizable if VVV has a basis consisting of eigenvectors of TTT. Equivalently, if the matrix M(T)\Mat(T)M(T) is diagonal in some basis.

The two formulations agree, because the matrix of the operator TTT in a basis v1,…,vnv_1,\dots,v_nv1​,…,vn​ is diagonal exactly when Tvk=λkvkTv_k=\lambda_kv_kTvk​=λk​vk​ for each kkk, i.e. when every basis vector is an eigenvector. The next theorem collects convenient conditions for diagonalizability.

Theorem 6.2 (Conditions for diagonalizability). Let dim⁡V=n\dim V=ndimV=n, and let λ1,…,λm\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_mλ1​,…,λm​ be all the distinct eigenvalues of an operator T∈L(V)T\in\Lin(V)T∈L(V). Then the following statements are equivalent:

  1. TTT is diagonalizable.

  2. VVV has a basis of eigenvectors of TTT.

  3. V=E(λ1,T)⊕⋯⊕E(λm,T)V=E(\lambda_1,T)\dsum\cdots\dsum E(\lambda_m,T)V=E(λ1​,T)⊕⋯⊕E(λm​,T).

  4. dim⁡V=dim⁡E(λ1,T)+⋯+dim⁡E(λm,T)\dim V=\dim E(\lambda_1,T)+\cdots+\dim E(\lambda_m,T)dimV=dimE(λ1​,T)+⋯+dimE(λm​,T).

Proof. The first two statements are equivalent by definition. By the corollary “The sum of eigenspaces is direct” of Lecture 5, the sum E(λ1,T)+⋯+E(λm,T)E(\lambda_1,T)+\cdots+E(\lambda_m,T)E(λ1​,T)+⋯+E(λm​,T) is direct, so its dimension equals ∑kdim⁡E(λk,T)\sum_k\dim E(\lambda_k,T)∑k​dimE(λk​,T) and is at most nnn.

Suppose VVV has a basis of eigenvectors. Each of its vectors lies in some eigenspace, so ∑kdim⁡E(λk,T)≥n\sum_k\dim E(\lambda_k,T)\ge n∑k​dimE(λk​,T)≥n. Together with the reverse inequality this gives equality of the dimensions.

If the dimensions add up to nnn, then the dimension of the direct sum equals dim⁡V\dim VdimV, and a subspace of full dimension is the whole space VVV.

Finally, if VVV is the direct sum of the eigenspaces, then joining bases of the eigenspaces gives a basis of VVV consisting of eigenvectors. 

Corollary 6.3 (Distinct eigenvalues suffice). If T∈L(V)T\in\Lin(V)T∈L(V) has dim⁡V\dim VdimV distinct eigenvalues, then TTT is diagonalizable.

Proof. Eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent (Lecture 5). We have dim⁡V\dim VdimV linearly independent vectors, so they form a basis. 

This condition is sufficient but not necessary: the identity operator has the single eigenvalue 111, yet its matrix is already diagonal. For a defective operator the dimensions of the eigenspaces add up to less than dim⁡V\dim VdimV, because some eigenspace is too small.

Example 6.4 (A diagonalizable operator). The matrix A=(2112)A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}A=(21​12​) has distinct eigenvalues 333 and 111 (Lecture 5), so by Corollary 6.3 it is diagonalizable. Its eigenpairs are λ1=3,  v1=(1,1) and λ2=1,  v2=(1,−1).\lambda_1=3,\;\allowbreak v_1=(1,1) \quad\allowbreak \text{ and }\quad\allowbreak \lambda_2=1,\;\allowbreak v_2=(1,-1).λ1​=3,v1​=(1,1) and λ2​=1,v2​=(1,−1). The matrix P=(111−1)P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}P=(11​1−1​) has these eigenvectors as its columns. The matrix PPP is the change-of-basis matrix from the eigenbasis to the standard basis, so P−1APP^{-1}APP−1AP is the matrix of the operator in the eigenbasis. The inverse formula for 2×22\times22×2 matrices gives P−1=12(111−1).P^{-1}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.P−1=21​(11​1−1​). Therefore P−1AP=12(111−1)(2112)(111−1)=(3001)=diag⁡(3,1).P^{-1}AP =\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\diag(3,1).P−1AP=21​(11​1−1​)(21​12​)(11​1−1​)=(30​01​)=diag(3,1). The diagonal holds the eigenvalues, in the same order as the eigenvectors in the columns of PPP.

Example 6.5 (A non-diagonalizable operator). The shear T=(1101)T=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)T=(10​11​) has the single eigenvalue 111, and its eigenspace E(1,T)=span⁡((1,0))E(1,T)=\spn\bigl((1,0)\bigr)E(1,T)=span((1,0)) is one-dimensional. The dimensions of the eigenspaces add up to 1<21<21<2, so the shear is not diagonalizable: there is no basis of eigenvectors.

Example 6.7 (A complete diagonalization). Let us diagonalize the matrix A=(4123).A=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}.A=(42​13​). The characteristic polynomial is χA(λ)=λ2−7λ+10=(λ−2)(λ−5),\chi_A(\lambda)=\lambda^2-7\lambda+10=(\lambda-2)(\lambda-5),χA​(λ)=λ2−7λ+10=(λ−2)(λ−5), so the eigenvalues are 555 and 222. For λ=5\lambda=5λ=5 we reduce the matrix A−5IA-5IA−5I: [−112−2]  → RREF   [1−100]  ⟹  x1=x2.\left[\begin{array}{cc} -1&1\\ 2&-2 \end{array}\right] \;\xrightarrow{\ \text{RREF}\ }\; \left[\begin{array}{cc} \pivot{1}&-1\\ 0&0 \end{array}\right] \;\Longrightarrow\; x_1=x_2 .[−12​1−2​] RREF ​[10​−10​]⟹x1​=x2​. Setting x2=1x_2=1x2​=1, we get the eigenvector (1,1)(1,1)(1,1). For λ=2\lambda=2λ=2 we reduce the matrix A−2IA-2IA−2I: [2121]  → RREF   [11200]  ⟹  x1=−12x2.\left[\begin{array}{cc} 2&1\\ 2&1 \end{array}\right] \;\xrightarrow{\ \text{RREF}\ }\; \left[\begin{array}{cc} \pivot{1}&\frac12\\ 0&0 \end{array}\right] \;\Longrightarrow\; x_1=-\frac12x_2 .[22​11​] RREF ​[10​21​0​]⟹x1​=−21​x2​. Setting x2=−2x_2=-2x2​=−2, we get the eigenvector (1,−2)(1,-2)(1,−2). We write the eigenvectors into the columns of PPP and find the inverse by the 2×22\times22×2 formula: P=(111−2) and P−1=13(211−1).P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix} \quad\allowbreak \text{ and }\quad\allowbreak P^{-1}=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.P=(11​1−2​) and P−1=31​(21​1−1​). Therefore P−1AP=13(211−1)(4123)(111−2)=(5002).P^{-1}AP =\frac13\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}5&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.P−1AP=31​(21​1−1​)(42​13​)(11​1−2​)=(50​02​). This method works for every diagonalizable operator: find the characteristic polynomial, find the eigenspaces by Gaussian elimination, and assemble the matrix PPP.

Before you go on

1 A 3×3 matrix A has the eigenvalues 3, 2, 2, listed with multiplicity. Which condition is equivalent to A being diagonalizable?

Here is the hint. Try once more — the explanation comes after that. Diagonalizable means the eigenspace dimensions add up to 3. What is dim E(3,A)? The eigenvalue 3 has algebraic multiplicity 1, and geometric ≤ algebraic, so dim E(3,A)=1. Hence the dimensions add up to 3 exactly when dim E(2,A)=2. A repeated eigenvalue alone decides nothing: the lecture's [[3,1,0],[0,2,0],[0,0,2]] has dim E(2,A)=2 and diagonalizes, while [[3,0,0],[0,2,1],[0,0,2]] has dim E(2,A)=1 and does not. det A=3·2·2=12≠0 holds for both, so invertibility is not the condition.

Diagonalization in practice

Let TTT be a diagonalizable operator on Fn\F^nFn, with eigenvectors v1,…,vnv_1,\dots,v_nv1​,…,vn​ and eigenvalues λ1,…,λn\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_nλ1​,…,λn​. Let A=M(T)A=\Mat(T)A=M(T) be its matrix in the standard basis. Form the matrices P=(∣⋯∣v1⋯vn∣⋯∣)(eigenvectors as columns),D=diag⁡(λ1,…,λn).P=\begin{pmatrix}|&\cdots&| \\v_1&\cdots&v_n\\|&\cdots&|\end{pmatrix} \quad\allowbreak \text{(eigenvectors as columns)},\qquad\allowbreak D=\diag(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n).P=​∣v1​∣​⋯⋯⋯​∣vn​∣​​(eigenvectors as columns),D=diag(λ1​,…,λn​). The equalities Avk=λkvkAv_k=\lambda_kv_kAvk​=λk​vk​, written column by column, form the equality AP=PDAP=PDAP=PD. The matrix PPP is invertible, so A=PDP−1.(6.1) \tag{6.1} A=PDP^{-1}. A=PDP−1.(6.1) This is the change-of-basis formula of Lecture 4, applied to the eigenbasis (Figure 1). It lets us compute powers, and soon functions, on the diagonal alone: Ak=(PDP−1)k=PDkP−1=Pdiag⁡(λ1k,…,λnk) P−1,A^k=(PDP^{-1})^k=PD^kP^{-1} =P\diag(\lambda_1^k,\dots,\lambda_n^k)\,P^{-1},Ak=(PDP−1)k=PDkP−1=Pdiag(λ1k​,…,λnk​)P−1, because the middle factors P−1PP^{-1}PP−1P cancel.

Example 6.8 (Computing a power). In Example 6.4 we found the matrices PPP, P−1P^{-1}P−1 and D=diag⁡(3,1)D=\diag(3,1)D=diag(3,1) for the matrix A=(2112)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)A=(21​12​), so Ak=12(111−1)(3k001)(111−1)=12(3k+13k−13k−13k+1).A^k=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}3^k&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix} =\frac12\begin{pmatrix}3^k+1&3^k-1\\3^k-1&3^k+1\end{pmatrix}.Ak=21​(11​1−1​)(3k0​01​)(11​1−1​)=21​(3k+13k−1​3k−13k+1​). Computing AkA^{k}Ak directly for large kkk would take far longer.

Remark 6.9 (Decoupling the equations). In physics, passing to the eigenbasis decouples the equations. A system of coupled linear differential equations x˙=Ax\dot x=Axx˙=Ax becomes, in the eigen-coordinates y=P−1xy=P^{-1}xy=P−1x, a set of independent equations y˙k=λkyk\dot y_k=\lambda_ky_ky˙​k​=λk​yk​. For a vibrating system x¨=−Kx\ddot x=-Kxx¨=−Kx the same decoupling gives the normal modes: each of them oscillates independently of the others (Example 6.10).

How to read phase space.

Consider a particle moving in a plane through a very viscous liquid. The friction is so strong that we can neglect the particle’s inertia: its velocity is proportional to the force acting on it. Let the matrix A=(2112)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)A=(21​12​) describe the force on the particle: at the point xxx the force is AxAxAx (in suitable units). Then the particle’s equation of motion is x˙=Ax\dot x=Axx˙=Ax. This force pushes the particle away from the origin. The eigenpairs of AAA are 3, (1,1)3,\ (1,1)3, (1,1) and 1, (1,−1)1,\ (1,-1)1, (1,−1), so on the eigenlines the force points straight away from the origin: on the line span⁡((1,1))\spn\bigl((1,1)\bigr)span((1,1)) it equals 3x3x3x, and on the line span⁡((1,−1))\spn\bigl((1,-1)\bigr)span((1,−1)) only xxx.

The state of the particle at time ttt is a point in the plane, x(t)=(x1(t),x2(t))x(t)=\bigl(x_1(t),x_2(t)\bigr)x(t)=(x1​(t),x2​(t)), and the equation x˙=Ax\dot x=Axx˙=Ax says in which direction and how fast this point moves. The set of all states is called the phase space. Here it is the plane, because in a viscous liquid the state of the particle is given by its position alone. Suppose that at time t=0t=0t=0 the particle is at the point (−2,1)(-2,1)(−2,1), i.e. x(0)=(−2,1)x(0)=(-2,1)x(0)=(−2,1). Expand the initial state in the eigenbasis: (−2,1)=−12(1,1)−32(1,−1).(-2,1)=-\tfrac12(1,1)-\tfrac32(1,-1).(−2,1)=−21​(1,1)−23​(1,−1). In eigen-coordinates each equation y˙k=λkyk\dot y_k=\lambda_ky_ky˙​k​=λk​yk​ has the solution yk(t)=eλktyk(0)y_k(t)=e^{\lambda_kt}y_k(0)yk​(t)=eλk​tyk​(0), so x(t)=−12e3t(1,1)−32et(1,−1).x(t)=-\tfrac12e^{3t}(1,1)-\tfrac32e^{t}(1,-1).x(t)=−21​e3t(1,1)−23​et(1,−1). What does this mean for the particle? Both terms grow, so the particle moves away from the origin. At first it moves straight to the left, because its velocity is x˙(0)=Ax(0)=(−3,0)\dot x(0)=Ax(0)=(-3,0)x˙(0)=Ax(0)=(−3,0). Then the particle turns downward, and at time t=12ln⁡3t=\tfrac12\ln3t=21​ln3 it crosses the x1x_1x1​ axis at the point (−33,0)(-3\sqrt3,0)(−33​,0). The term with e3te^{3t}e3t grows faster, so after a long time the particle moves almost parallel to the vector (1,1)(1,1)(1,1), to the left and down, i.e. in the direction in which the force is strongest. From then on its distance and its speed grow roughly like e3te^{3t}e3t.

A drawing of the trajectories of several initial states is called a phase portrait. Every trajectory that does not start on an eigenline behaves in the same way (Figure 2): near the origin it is tangent to the slower eigendirection (1,−1)(1,-1)(1,−1), and far from the origin it moves almost parallel to the faster direction (1,1)(1,1)(1,1).

Example 6.10 (Normal modes of two coupled masses). Two equal masses are joined to each other by a spring, and each is tied to a wall by an identical spring. Their displacements obey the equation x¨=−Kx\ddot x=-Kxx¨=−Kx with K=(2−1−12)K=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)K=(2−1​−12​) (in suitable units). The eigenvalues of KKK are 111 and 333, and the eigenvectors are (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) and (1,−1)(1,-1)(1,−1). In these normal coordinates the system splits into two independent oscillators. The masses move together (the mode (1,1)(1,1)(1,1)) at angular frequency ω=1\omega=1ω=1, or in opposite directions (the mode (1,−1)(1,-1)(1,−1)) at frequency ω=3\omega=\sqrt3ω=3​ (Figure 3). Every motion is a sum of these modes. For example, pull the first mass aside by 111, hold the second in place, and release both from rest. Then x(0)=(1,0)=12(1,1)+12(1,−1)x(0)=(1,0)=\tfrac12(1,1)+\tfrac12(1,-1)x(0)=(1,0)=21​(1,1)+21​(1,−1) and x(t)=12cos⁡t (1,1)+12cos⁡3 t (1,−1).x(t)=\tfrac12\cos t\,(1,1)+\tfrac12\cos\sqrt3\,t\,(1,-1).x(t)=21​cost(1,1)+21​cos3​t(1,−1). The oscillation passes back and forth between the two masses. So diagonalizing the matrix KKK is exactly finding the normal modes.

The Cayley–Hamilton theorem

The Cayley–Hamilton theorem relates an operator to its characteristic polynomial χT(λ)=det⁡(λI−T)\chi_T(\lambda)=\det(\lambda I-T)χT​(λ)=det(λI−T). In the general case its proof rests on the upper-triangular matrix (Lecture 5) and the following lemma.

Lemma 6.11 (The product of the triangular factors is zero [self-study]). Suppose TTT has an upper-triangular matrix with diagonal entries λ1,…,λn\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_nλ1​,…,λn​ with respect to a basis v1,…,vnv_1,\dots,v_nv1​,…,vn​. Then (T−λ1I)(T−λ2I)⋯(T−λnI)=0.(T-\lambda_1I)(T-\lambda_2I)\cdots(T-\lambda_nI)=0 .(T−λ1​I)(T−λ2​I)⋯(T−λn​I)=0.

Proof. The matrix is upper triangular, so each factor T−λkIT-\lambda_kIT−λk​I maps the vector vkv_kvk​ into a smaller subspace: (T−λkI)vk∈span⁡(v1,…,vk−1).(T-\lambda_kI)v_k\in\spn(v_1,\dots,v_{k-1}).(T−λk​I)vk​∈span(v1​,…,vk−1​). We prove by induction on kkk that the product of the first kkk factors maps the vectors v1,…,vkv_1,\dots,v_kv1​,…,vk​ to zero.

  1. For k=1k=1k=1, (T−λ1I)v1=0(T-\lambda_1I)v_1=0(T−λ1​I)v1​=0.

  2. Suppose the product of the first k−1k-1k−1 factors maps the vectors v1,…,vk−1v_1,\dots,v_{k-1}v1​,…,vk−1​ to zero.

  3. The rightmost factor T−λkIT-\lambda_kIT−λk​I acts on the vector vkv_kvk​ first. It maps vkv_kvk​ into the subspace span⁡(v1,…,vk−1)\spn(v_1,\dots,v_{k-1})span(v1​,…,vk−1​), which the remaining factors map to zero by the induction hypothesis. All the factors commute, because they are polynomials in the operator TTT. So we may apply the first k−1k-1k−1 factors first; they map the vectors v1,…,vk−1v_1,\dots,v_{k-1}v1​,…,vk−1​ to zero.

  4. For k=nk=nk=n, the whole product maps every basis vector to zero, so it is the zero operator.

 

Theorem 6.12 (Cayley–Hamilton). Every operator TTT on a finite-dimensional vector space over F\FF satisfies its own characteristic equation: χT(T)=0.\chi_T(T)=0.χT​(T)=0.

Proof for diagonalizable TTT. Write A=PDP−1A=PDP^{-1}A=PDP−1, where D=diag⁡(λ1,…,λn)D=\diag(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)D=diag(λ1​,…,λn​). For any polynomial ppp we have p(A)=P p(D) P−1p(A)=P\,p(D)\,P^{-1}p(A)=Pp(D)P−1 and p(D)=diag⁡(p(λ1),…,p(λn))p(D)=\diag(p(\lambda_1),\dots,p(\lambda_n))p(D)=diag(p(λ1​),…,p(λn​)). Take p=χAp=\chi_Ap=χA​. Each eigenvalue λk\lambda_kλk​ is a root of the polynomial χA\chi_AχA​, so χA(A)=Pdiag⁡(χA(λ1),…,χA(λn))P−1=Pdiag⁡(0,…,0) P−1=0.\chi_A(A)=P\diag\bigl(\chi_A(\lambda_1),\dots,\chi_A(\lambda_n)\bigr)P^{-1} =P\diag(0,\dots,0)\,P^{-1}=0 . χA​(A)=Pdiag(χA​(λ1​),…,χA​(λn​))P−1=Pdiag(0,…,0)P−1=0. 

Proof in general (self-study). Over C\CC every operator has an upper-triangular matrix with diagonal entries λ1,…,λn\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_nλ1​,…,λn​ (Lecture 5, where only a sketch of the proof is given). Then χT(λ)=(λ−λ1)⋯(λ−λn)\chi_T(\lambda)=(\lambda-\lambda_1)\cdots(\lambda-\lambda_n)χT​(λ)=(λ−λ1​)⋯(λ−λn​). By Lemma 6.11, (T−λ1I)⋯(T−λnI)=0(T-\lambda_1I)\cdots(T-\lambda_nI)=0(T−λ1​I)⋯(T−λn​I)=0, and this product is exactly χT(T)\chi_T(T)χT​(T). Therefore χT(T)=0\chi_T(T)=0χT​(T)=0.

A real matrix can also be regarded as a complex matrix. For it the identity χT(T)=0\chi_T(T)=0χT​(T)=0 is already proved. Both sides of this identity are real matrices, so the identity also holds over R\RR. 

Corollary 6.13 (Inverse and powers as low-degree polynomials). Let TTT be invertible, and let χT(λ)=λn+cn−1λn−1+⋯+c1λ+c0\chi_T(\lambda)=\lambda^n+c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1\lambda+c_0χT​(λ)=λn+cn−1​λn−1+⋯+c1​λ+c0​ (so c0=(−1)ndet⁡T≠0c_0=(-1)^n\det T\neq0c0​=(−1)ndetT=0). Then T−1=−1c0(Tn−1+cn−1Tn−2+⋯+c1I).T^{-1}=-\frac1{c_0}\bigl(T^{n-1}+c_{n-1}T^{n-2}+\cdots+c_1I\bigr).T−1=−c0​1​(Tn−1+cn−1​Tn−2+⋯+c1​I). More generally, every power TkT^kTk with k≥nk\ge nk≥n can be written as a polynomial in TTT of degree less than nnn.

Proof. By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, Tn+⋯+c1T+c0I=0T^n+\cdots+c_1T+c_0I=0Tn+⋯+c1​T+c0​I=0. Moving c0Ic_0Ic0​I to the other side and multiplying by T−1/(−c0)T^{-1}/(-c_0)T−1/(−c0​) gives the first claim. The same equality expresses TnT^nTn through lower powers, and by induction so is every higher power. 

Example 6.14 (Inverse matrix from Cayley–Hamilton). Let A=(2112)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)A=(21​12​). Then χA(λ)=λ2−4λ+3\chi_A(\lambda)=\lambda^2-4\lambda+3χA​(λ)=λ2−4λ+3, so A2−4A+3I=0A^2-4A+3I=0A2−4A+3I=0 and A−1=13(4I−A)=13(2−1−12).A^{-1}=\frac13(4I-A)=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}.A−1=31​(4I−A)=31​(2−1​−12​). Example 6.16 (Reducing a high power). In Example 6.15 we obtained A2=5A+2IA^2=5A+2IA2=5A+2I. So we can write every higher power as a linear combination of the matrices AAA and III: A3=A⋅A2=5A2+2A=5(5A+2I)+2A=27A+10I,A^3=A\cdot A^2=5A^2+2A=5(5A+2I)+2A=27A+10I,A3=A⋅A2=5A2+2A=5(5A+2I)+2A=27A+10I, and by induction Ak=αkA+βkIA^k=\alpha_kA+\beta_kIAk=αk​A+βk​I with scalars αk,βk\alpha_k,\beta_kαk​,βk​. Thus any power of the matrix AAA is written with just two matrices, III and AAA.

Remark 6.17 (Minimal polynomial [self-study]). The polynomial of least degree with leading coefficient 111 that satisfies mT(T)=0m_T(T)=0mT​(T)=0 is called the minimal polynomial mTm_TmT​ of the operator TTT. The characteristic polynomial χT\chi_TχT​ is divisible by mTm_TmT​. The roots of mTm_TmT​ that lie in the field F\FF are exactly the eigenvalues of TTT over F\FF. Over R\RR, quadratic factors that cannot be split may remain. The criterion for diagonalizability that takes the field into account is T is diagonalizable over F⟺mT(x) splits over Finto a product of distinct linear factors.T\text{ is diagonalizable over }\F \quad\allowbreak \Longleftrightarrow\quad\allowbreak \substack{m_T(x)\text{ splits over }\F\\ \text{into a product of distinct linear factors}.}T is diagonalizable over F⟺mT​(x) splits over Finto a product of distinct linear factors.​ The minimal polynomial mT(x)=x2+1m_T(x)=x^2+1mT​(x)=x2+1 of the rotation of the plane through a right angle has no repeated roots, but it does not split over R\RR, so this rotation is not diagonalizable over R\RR. Over C\CC the polynomial splits as (x−i)(x+i)(x-i)(x+i)(x−i)(x+i), and the rotation is diagonalizable. The minimal polynomial of the shear A=(1101)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)A=(10​11​) is (x−1)2(x-1)^2(x−1)2, because A−I≠0A-I\neq0A−I=0 but (A−I)2=0(A-I)^2=0(A−I)2=0. The repeated factor prevents the shear from being diagonalized, as in Example 6.5. Finally, if dim⁡V=n\dim V=ndimV=n and TTT has nnn distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λn\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_nλ1​,…,λn​ in the field F\FF, then mT(x)=∏k=1n(x−λk)m_T(x)=\prod_{k=1}^n(x-\lambda_k)mT​(x)=∏k=1n​(x−λk​). This agrees with Corollary 6.3.

Before you go on

2 A matrix A satisfies A²−5A+6I=0. Which matrix is A⁻¹?

Here is the hint. Try once more — the explanation comes after that. Move the constant term to the other side and factor out A. A²−5A=−6I, i.e. A(A−5I)=−6I. Dividing by −6 gives A·(5I−A)/6=I, so A⁻¹=(5I−A)/6. The option (A²−5A)/6 is just −I.

Functions of operators

We have already used polynomials of an operator. To a diagonalizable operator TTT we can apply any function defined at its eigenvalues.

Definition 6.18 (Function of a diagonalizable operator). Let T=PDP−1T=PDP^{-1}T=PDP−1, where D=diag⁡(λ1,…,λn)D=\diag(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)D=diag(λ1​,…,λn​), and let the function fff be defined at every point λk\lambda_kλk​. Define f(T)=P f(D) P−1,f(D)=diag⁡(f(λ1),…,f(λn)).f(T)=P\,f(D)\,P^{-1},\qquad\allowbreak f(D)=\diag\bigl(f(\lambda_1),\dots,f(\lambda_n)\bigr).f(T)=Pf(D)P−1,f(D)=diag(f(λ1​),…,f(λn​)). This definition agrees with the power-series definition whenever the series converges, and it does not depend on the choice of eigenbasis.

The most important example is the exponential. It is defined for every square matrix by the series eA=∑k=0∞Akk!.e^{A}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{A^k}{k!}.eA=k=0∑∞​k!Ak​. We read this series componentwise. Each of the n2n^2n2 entries is an ordinary complex power series whose terms are bounded by the terms of a scalar exponential series, so it converges. Nothing more is needed below. In Lecture 7 we introduce norms; then convergence can be studied for the matrices themselves rather than for their entries. For a diagonalizable matrix A=PDP−1A=PDP^{-1}A=PDP−1 the sum of the series is eA=Pdiag⁡(eλ1,…,eλn) P−1e^{A}=P\diag(e^{\lambda_1},\dots,e^{\lambda_n})\,P^{-1}eA=Pdiag(eλ1​,…,eλn​)P−1. For dynamics, the most important property of the exponential is the following.

Proposition 6.19 (Exponential and linear dynamics). For a fixed matrix AAA the function t↦etAt\mapsto e^{tA}t↦etA satisfies ddtetA=A etA and e0A=I.\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=A\,e^{tA}\quad\allowbreak \text{ and }\quad\allowbreak e^{0A}=I.dtd​etA=AetA and e0A=I. Proof. We differentiate the series term by term, componentwise: ddt∑ktkAkk!=∑k≥1tk−1Ak(k−1)!=A etA.\frac{d}{dt}\sum_k\frac{t^kA^k}{k!} =\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{t^{k-1}A^k}{(k-1)!}=A\,e^{tA}.dtd​k∑​k!tkAk​=k≥1∑​(k−1)!tk−1Ak​=AetA. Then ddt(etAx0)=AetAx0\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(e^{tA}x_0\bigr)=A e^{tA}x_0dtd​(etAx0​)=AetAx0​ and x(0)=x0x(0)=x_0x(0)=x0​.

Uniqueness. Suppose x(t)x(t)x(t) is any solution with the same initial value. The matrix AAA commutes with its power series, so ddt(e−tAx(t))=−Ae−tAx(t)+e−tAAx(t)=0.\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(e^{-tA}x(t)\bigr) =-Ae^{-tA}x(t)+e^{-tA}Ax(t)=0.dtd​(e−tAx(t))=−Ae−tAx(t)+e−tAAx(t)=0. Thus e−tAx(t)=x0e^{-tA}x(t)=x_0e−tAx(t)=x0​. Multiplying by etAe^{tA}etA, we get x(t)=etAx0x(t)=e^{tA}x_0x(t)=etAx0​.

Example 6.21 (Solving an initial value problem). For the same matrix AAA with the initial condition x(0)=(1,0)x(0)=(1,0)x(0)=(1,0), we expand the initial value in the eigenbasis: x(0)=12(1,1)+12(1,−1).x(0)=\tfrac12(1,1)+\tfrac12(1,-1).x(0)=21​(1,1)+21​(1,−1). Example 6.22 (Spin rotation: eiθσxe^{i\theta\sigma_x}eiθσx​). Since σx2=I\sigma_x^2=Iσx2​=I, the exponential series splits into even and odd powers: eiθσx=∑j(iθ)2j(2j)!I+∑j(iθ)2j+1(2j+1)!σx=cos⁡θ I+isin⁡θ σx.e^{i\theta\sigma_x} =\sum_{j}\frac{(i\theta)^{2j}}{(2j)!}I +\sum_{j}\frac{(i\theta)^{2j+1}}{(2j+1)!}\sigma_x =\cos\theta\,I+i\sin\theta\,\sigma_x .eiθσx​=j∑​(2j)!(iθ)2j​I+j∑​(2j+1)!(iθ)2j+1​σx​=cosθI+isinθσx​. Example 6.23 (Square root of an operator). The matrix A=(2112)=PDP−1A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)=PDP^{-1}A=(21​12​)=PDP−1, where D=diag⁡(3,1)D=\diag(3,1)D=diag(3,1), has positive eigenvalues. So it has the square root A=Pdiag⁡(3,1) P−1=12(3+13−13−13+1),\sqrt{A}=P\diag(\sqrt3,1)\,P^{-1} =\frac12\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt3+1&\sqrt3-1\\\sqrt3-1&\sqrt3+1\end{pmatrix},A​=Pdiag(3​,1)P−1=21​(3​+13​−1​3​−13​+1​), which satisfies (A)2=A(\sqrt A)^2=A(A​)2=A. Computing a function of an operator is no harder than computing the same function of its eigenvalues.

Remark 6.24 (Identities hold for operators too). Every identity between functions also holds for diagonalizable operators, because both sides are computed separately for each eigenvalue. For example, sin⁡2A+cos⁡2A=I\sin^2A+\cos^2A=Isin2A+cos2A=I and eAe−A=Ie^{A}e^{-A}=IeAe−A=I hold for every diagonalizable matrix AAA.

Proposition 6.25 (Spectral decomposition). Let TTT be diagonalizable, and let λ1,…,λm\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_mλ1​,…,λm​ be all its distinct eigenvalues. Then there exist projections P1,…,PmP_1,\dots,P_mP1​,…,Pm​ satisfying PiPj=0  (i≠j),P1+⋯+Pm=I,T=λ1P1+⋯+λmPm.P_iP_j=0\ \ (i\neq j),\qquad\allowbreak P_1+\cdots+P_m=I,\qquad\allowbreak T=\lambda_1P_1+\cdots+\lambda_mP_m .Pi​Pj​=0  (i=j),P1​+⋯+Pm​=I,T=λ1​P1​+⋯+λm​Pm​. The projection PkP_kPk​ leaves the vectors of E(λk,T)E(\lambda_k,T)E(λk​,T) unchanged and maps the vectors of the other eigenspaces to zero. Moreover, f(T)=∑kf(λk)Pkf(T)=\sum_k f(\lambda_k)P_kf(T)=∑k​f(λk​)Pk​ for any function fff defined on the set spec⁡(T)\spec(T)spec(T).

Proof. In the eigenbasis, the operator TTT acts on each eigenspace block as multiplication by λk\lambda_kλk​. Let PkP_kPk​ be the projection that picks out the block of E(λk,T)E(\lambda_k,T)E(λk​,T). These projections satisfy the stated relations, and T=∑kλkPkT=\sum_k\lambda_kP_kT=∑k​λk​Pk​. Applying the function fff to each block, we get f(T)=∑kf(λk)Pkf(T)=\sum_k f(\lambda_k)P_kf(T)=∑k​f(λk​)Pk​. 

In Lecture 10 we prove the spectral theorem. It implies that for operators corresponding to observables the projections PkP_kPk​ are orthogonal; orthogonality is defined in Lecture 7.

Example 6.26 (Spectral decomposition in coordinates). The projections of the matrix A=(2112)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)A=(21​12​) onto the eigenspaces E(3,A)=span⁡((1,1))E(3,A)=\spn\bigl((1,1)\bigr)E(3,A)=span((1,1)) and E(1,A)=span⁡((1,−1))E(1,A)=\spn\bigl((1,-1)\bigr)E(1,A)=span((1,−1)) are P1=12(1111),P2=12(1−1−11),P_1=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\allowbreak P_2=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix},P1​=21​(11​11​),P2​=21​(1−1​−11​), and P1+P2=IP_1+P_2=IP1​+P2​=I, P1P2=0P_1P_2=0P1​P2​=0. Then A=3P1+P2A=3P_1+P_2A=3P1​+P2​, and by Proposition 6.25, Ak=3kP1+P2A^k=3^kP_1+P_2Ak=3kP1​+P2​ and eA=e3P1+eP2e^{A}=e^3P_1+eP_2eA=e3P1​+eP2​ with no matrix multiplication at all. Spectral mapping and time evolution

How do the eigenvalues change when we apply a function to an operator?

Proposition 6.27 (Spectral mapping). If TTT is diagonalizable over F\FF and f:spec⁡(T)→Ff:\spec(T)\to\Ff:spec(T)→F, then spec⁡(f(T))={f(λ):λ∈spec⁡(T)},\spec\bigl(f(T)\bigr)=\set{f(\lambda):\lambda\in\spec(T)},spec(f(T))={f(λ):λ∈spec(T)}, and every eigenvector of TTT for λ\lambdaλ is an eigenvector of f(T)f(T)f(T) for f(λ)f(\lambda)f(λ).

Proof. Let Tv=λvTv=\lambda vTv=λv. In eigen-coordinates the nonzero coordinates of vvv sit only in the positions where the diagonal of DDD holds λ\lambdaλ, and f(D)f(D)f(D) multiplies each of them by f(λ)f(\lambda)f(λ). Therefore f(T)v=Pf(D)P−1vf(T)v=Pf(D)P^{-1}vf(T)v=Pf(D)P−1v is the vector vvv multiplied by f(λ)f(\lambda)f(λ). Conversely, the same eigenbasis also diagonalizes f(T)f(T)f(T), and its diagonal holds exactly the values f(λk)f(\lambda_k)f(λk​). So f(T)f(T)f(T) has no other eigenvalues. 

The converse fails: if fff is not injective on spec⁡(T)\spec(T)spec(T), an eigenvector of f(T)f(T)f(T) need not be an eigenvector of TTT. For example, for T=diag⁡(1,−1)T=\diag(1,-1)T=diag(1,−1) and f(λ)=λ2f(\lambda)=\lambda^2f(λ)=λ2 we get f(T)=If(T)=If(T)=I. Every nonzero vector is an eigenvector of III, while TTT has only two eigendirections.

Example 6.28 (Spectrum of a function). The spectrum of the matrix A=(2112)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)A=(21​12​) is {1,3}\set{1,3}{1,3}. So the spectrum of eAe^{A}eA is {e, e3}\set{e,\,e^{3}}{e,e3}, and that of A10A^{10}A10 is {1, 310}\set{1,\,3^{10}}{1,310}. The eigenvectors are the same throughout: (1,−1)(1,-1)(1,−1) and (1,1)(1,1)(1,1). Once the eigenvectors are found, we need not recompute them for any function of AAA.

Example 6.29 (Imaginary eigenvalues produce oscillation). The eigenvalues of the matrix A=(0−ωω0)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-\omega\\\omega&0\end{smallmatrix} \right)A=(0ω​−ω0​) are ±iω\pm i\omega±iω. Since A2=−ω2IA^2=-\omega^2 IA2=−ω2I, the exponential series splits into even and odd powers, as in Example 6.22, and etA=(cos⁡ωt−sin⁡ωtsin⁡ωtcos⁡ωt).e^{tA}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\omega t&-\sin\omega t\\ \sin\omega t&\cos\omega t\end{pmatrix}.etA=(cosωtsinωt​−sinωtcosωt​). So the equation x˙=Ax\dot x=Axx˙=Ax describes rotation at angular frequency ω\omegaω. For example, when x(0)=(1,0)x(0)=(1,0)x(0)=(1,0), the state x(t)=(cos⁡ωt,sin⁡ωt)x(t)=(\cos\omega t,\sin\omega t)x(t)=(cosωt,sinωt) goes round a circle, and both of its coordinates oscillate harmonically (Figure 4). Imaginary eigenvalues produce oscillation, while the real ones in Example 6.20 produced growth. This is how linear algebra describes harmonic oscillation.

Remark 6.30 (Quantum time evolution). A quantum state evolves in time by the law ∣ψ(t)⟩=e−iH^t/ℏ∣ψ(0)⟩.\ket{\psi(t)}=e^{-i\hat Ht/\hbar}\ket{\psi(0)}.∣ψ(t)⟩=e−iH^t/ℏ∣ψ(0)⟩. In the energy eigenbasis H^=diag⁡(E1,…,En)\hat H=\diag(E_1,\dots,E_n)H^=diag(E1​,…,En​), so e−iH^t/ℏ=diag⁡(e−iE1t/ℏ,…,e−iEnt/ℏ).e^{-i\hat Ht/\hbar}=\diag\bigl(e^{-iE_1t/\hbar},\dots,e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}\bigr).e−iH^t/ℏ=diag(e−iE1​t/ℏ,…,e−iEn​t/ℏ). Over time, each state of definite energy only acquires a phase factor e−iEnt/ℏe^{-iE_nt/\hbar}e−iEn​t/ℏ, and a general state is a superposition of such states. So diagonalizing the Hamiltonian means solving the dynamics. That the Hamiltonian can always be diagonalized we prove in Lecture 10 (the spectral theorem).

Proposition 6.31 (Commuting operators share an eigenvector). If VVV is a nonzero finite-dimensional complex vector space and S,T∈L(V)S,T\in\Lin(V)S,T∈L(V) commute, then SSS and TTT have a common eigenvector.

Proof.

  1. By the theorem “Eigenvalues exist over C\CC” of Lecture 5, the operator SSS has an eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ.

  2. Its eigenspace is invariant under TTT. Indeed, for v∈E(λ,S)v\in E(\lambda,S)v∈E(λ,S), S(Tv)=T(Sv)=T(λv)=λ(Tv).S(Tv)=T(Sv)=T(\lambda v)=\lambda(Tv).S(Tv)=T(Sv)=T(λv)=λ(Tv). So Tv∈E(λ,S)Tv\in E(\lambda,S)Tv∈E(λ,S).

  3. The subspace E(λ,S)E(\lambda,S)E(λ,S) is invariant, so we may regard TTT as an operator on this subspace. It is a nonzero complex space, so by the same theorem it contains an eigenvector vvv of TTT.

  4. The vector vvv is an eigenvector of TTT. It lies in the subspace E(λ,S)E(\lambda,S)E(λ,S), so it is also an eigenvector of SSS.

 

Triangularization is not diagonalization.

Repeating this argument with invariant subspaces, we can prove more: commuting complex operators  ⟹  simultaneous upper triangularization.\text{commuting complex operators} \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{simultaneous upper triangularization}.commuting complex operators⟹simultaneous upper triangularization. This means that there is a basis in which the matrices of both operators are upper triangular (Lecture 5, Section 6). Commuting is not enough for simultaneous diagonalization: both operators must also be diagonalizable. For example, the identity operator commutes with every operator, including the shear of Example 6.5. Yet these two operators cannot be diagonalized simultaneously.

Remark 6.32 (Simultaneous diagonalization). The matrices of commuting diagonalizable operators are diagonal in one basis, consisting of common eigenvectors (cf. Proposition 6.31). In physics this means that compatible observables can be measured precisely together.

Example 6.33 (Compatible and incompatible observables). Compare the Pauli matrices σx=(0110) and σz=(100−1).\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix} \quad\allowbreak \text{ and }\quad\allowbreak \sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.σx​=(01​10​) and σz​=(10​0−1​). The eigenvectors of σz\sigma_zσz​ are (1,0)(1,0)(1,0) and (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), but neither of them is an eigenvector of σx\sigma_xσx​. Multiplying the matrices, we get σxσz=(0−110)≠(01−10)=σzσx.\sigma_x\sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix} \neq\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}=\sigma_z\sigma_x.σx​σz​=(01​−10​)=(0−1​10​)=σz​σx​.

Interpretation.

Commuting diagonalizable operators have a common eigenbasis (see the remark above). These two matrices do not commute and have no common eigenbasis. In physics this means that the spin projections on the xxx and zzz axes cannot be measured precisely together. This is the uncertainty relation, which we discuss in Lecture 9.

When diagonalization fails [self-study]

Not every operator is diagonalizable. In that case generalized eigenvectors, which we define below, come to the rescue. The obstruction to diagonalization is the nilpotent part of the operator. An operator NNN is called nilpotent if Nk=0N^k=0Nk=0 for some kkk; no change of basis can remove such a part. Suppose an operator has a single eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ and A=λI+NA=\lambda I+NA=λI+N, where NNN is nilpotent. The matrices λI\lambda IλI and NNN commute, so the exponential series terminates: etA=eλt etN=eλt(I+tN+t22!N2+⋯+tk−1(k−1)!Nk−1).e^{tA}=e^{\lambda t}\,e^{tN} =e^{\lambda t}\Bigl(I+tN+\tfrac{t^2}{2!}N^2+\cdots+\tfrac{t^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}N^{k-1}\Bigr).etA=eλtetN=eλt(I+tN+2!t2​N2+⋯+(k−1)!tk−1​Nk−1). For the shear-type matrix A=(λ10λ)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\lambda&1\\0&\lambda \end{smallmatrix}\right)A=(λ0​1λ​) the nilpotent part N=(0100)N=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0 \end{smallmatrix}\right)N=(00​10​) satisfies N2=0N^2=0N2=0, so etA=eλt(1t01).e^{tA}=e^{\lambda t}\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.etA=eλt(10​t1​). The extra factor ttt shows that the eigenvalue is defective. It gives the solutions t eλtt\,e^{\lambda t}teλt, the same ones that appear when the characteristic equation of a linear differential equation has a repeated root.

Generalized eigenvectors.

Definition 6.34 (Generalized eigenvectors and eigenspaces). A nonzero vector vvv is called a generalized eigenvector for the eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ if (T−λI)kv=0for some k≥1.(T-\lambda I)^kv=0 \qquad\allowbreak \text{for some }k\ge1.(T−λI)kv=0for some k≥1. The generalized eigenspace is the set G(λ,T)={v:(T−λI)kv=0 for some k}.G(\lambda,T)=\set{v:(T-\lambda I)^kv=0\text{ for some }k}.G(λ,T)={v:(T−λI)kv=0 for some k}. Clearly, E(λ,T)⊆G(λ,T).E(\lambda,T)\subseteq G(\lambda,T).E(λ,T)⊆G(λ,T).

There is no need to search for the exponent kkk: one fixed exponent is enough. Write N=T−λIN=T-\lambda IN=T−λI and n=dim⁡Vn=\dim Vn=dimV. The kernels grow: ker⁡N⊆ker⁡N2⊆⋯\ker N\subseteq\ker N^2\subseteq\cdotskerN⊆kerN2⊆⋯. This chain stops as soon as two consecutive kernels coincide. Indeed, suppose ker⁡Nj=ker⁡Nj+1\ker N^{j}=\ker N^{j+1}kerNj=kerNj+1 and Nj+2v=0N^{j+2}v=0Nj+2v=0. Then Nv∈ker⁡Nj+1=ker⁡NjNv\in\ker N^{j+1}=\ker N^{j}Nv∈kerNj+1=kerNj, so Nj+1v=Nj(Nv)=0N^{j+1}v=N^{j}(Nv)=0Nj+1v=Nj(Nv)=0. Hence ker⁡Nj+1=ker⁡Nj+2\ker N^{j+1}=\ker N^{j+2}kerNj+1=kerNj+2, and the same step repeats from there on. Until the chain stops, every inclusion is strict, so at each step the dimension grows by at least 111. The kernels are subspaces of VVV, so the chain stabilizes by the nnn-th step at the latest. Therefore G(λ,T)=ker⁡(T−λI)dim⁡V.G(\lambda,T)=\ker(T-\lambda I)^{\dim V}.G(λ,T)=ker(T−λI)dimV.

Theorem 6.35 (Generalized eigenspace decomposition). Let VVV be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, and let λ1,…,λr\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_rλ1​,…,λr​ be all the distinct eigenvalues of an operator TTT. Then for each eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ the dimension dim⁡G(λ,T)\dim G(\lambda,T)dimG(λ,T) of its generalized eigenspace equals its algebraic multiplicity, and VVV is the direct sum of the generalized eigenspaces: V=G(λ1,T)⊕⋯⊕G(λr,T).V=G(\lambda_1,T)\dsum\cdots\dsum G(\lambda_r,T).V=G(λ1​,T)⊕⋯⊕G(λr​,T).

Interpretation.

A defective operator may lack ordinary eigenvectors, but there are always enough generalized eigenvectors to span the whole space. This decomposition is the foundation of the Jordan form. We do not prove the theorem.

Example 6.36 (A generalized eigenvector). The only eigenspace of the shear T=(1101)T=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)T=(10​11​) is E(1,T)=span⁡((1,0)).E(1,T)=\spn((1,0)).E(1,T)=span((1,0)). However, (T−I)2=0,G(1,T)=ker⁡(T−I)2=C2.(T-I)^2=0, \qquad\allowbreak G(1,T)=\ker(T-I)^2=\C^2.(T−I)2=0,G(1,T)=ker(T−I)2=C2. For example, the operator T−IT-IT−I maps the vector (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) to the eigenvector (1,0)(1,0)(1,0), and this one to the zero vector: (0,1)↦ T−I (1,0)↦ T−I 0.(0,1)\xmapsto{\,T-I\,}(1,0)\xmapsto{\,T-I\,}0.(0,1)T−I​(1,0)T−I​0. Such a sequence of vectors is called a Jordan chain. It leads from a generalized eigenvector to an ordinary eigenvector.

Theorem 6.37 (Jordan normal form). Every operator on a finite-dimensional complex space has a basis of generalized eigenvectors in which its matrix is block diagonal, each block being a Jordan block J=λI+N,N=(010⋱⋱10).J=\lambda I+N,\qquad\allowbreak N=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&&\\[-0.5em]&0&\ddots&\\[-0.5em]&&\ddots&1\\&&&0\end{pmatrix}.J=λI+N,N=​0​10​⋱⋱​10​​. The block has the eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ on its diagonal, and above the diagonal the ones of the nilpotent shift NNN. Each block corresponds to one Jordan chain of generalized eigenvectors (Example 6.36).

The shift NNN maps each basis vector of the block to the previous one, ej↦ej−1↦⋯↦e1↦0e_j\mapsto e_{j-1}\mapsto\cdots\mapsto e_1\mapsto0ej​↦ej−1​↦⋯↦e1​↦0. After finitely many steps only the zero vector remains; this is what it means for NNN to be nilpotent.

Theorem 6.38 (Jordan–Chevalley decomposition). On a finite-dimensional complex vector space every operator AAA can be written uniquely as a sum A=D+N,DN=ND,A=D+N,\qquad\allowbreak DN=ND,A=D+N,DN=ND, where DDD is diagonalizable, NNN is nilpotent, and DDD and NNN are polynomials in AAA.

Since DDD and NNN are polynomials in AAA, they commute with every matrix that commutes with AAA. So the decomposition preserves all the symmetries of AAA. It is also the most convenient way to compute etA=etDetNe^{tA}=e^{tD}e^{tN}etA=etDetN for any matrix: the diagonalizable part gives oscillation and decay, and the nilpotent part gives corrections polynomial in ttt.

Remark 6.39 (Nilpotent operators and ladder operators). In physics, nilpotent operators appear as ladder operators on finite-dimensional spaces. On the state space of spin jjj (of dimension 2j+12j+12j+1) the raising operator J+J_+J+​ maps ∣m⟩↦∣m+1⟩\ket m\mapsto\ket{m+1}∣m⟩↦∣m+1⟩, and it maps the top state to zero. Therefore J+ 2j+1=0J_+^{\,2j+1}=0J+2j+1​=0: J+J_+J+​ is nilpotent, and it acts exactly like the shift NNN of a Jordan block. The lowering operator of the harmonic oscillator, truncated to NNN levels, is nilpotent in the same way (aN=0a^N=0aN=0). The untruncated oscillator is discussed in Lectures 13–14.

Remark 6.40 (Where defective operators occur in physics). Operators corresponding to observables are always diagonalizable (Lectures 9–10), so there are no defective operators among them. Defective operators occur in systems that lose energy. For example, the repeated root of a critically damped oscillator gives the solution t e−γtt\,e^{-\gamma t}te−γt, similar to the t eλtt\,e^{\lambda t}teλt obtained above. Here we only state the Jordan form and the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition, without proving their construction. Later we use only the principle: diagonalize when possible, and otherwise add a nilpotent correction.

An operator is diagonalizable if and only if it has an eigenbasis, i.e. if the dimensions of its eigenspaces add up to dim⁡V\dim VdimV. A convenient sufficient condition: dim⁡V\dim VdimV distinct eigenvalues.

In an eigenbasis A=PDP−1A=PDP^{-1}A=PDP−1, so powers and functions are computed separately for each eigenvalue: Ak=PDkP−1A^k=PD^kP^{-1}Ak=PDkP−1 and f(T)=Pf(D)P−1f(T)=Pf(D)P^{-1}f(T)=Pf(D)P−1. The exponential etAe^{tA}etA solves the equation x˙=Ax\dot x=Axx˙=Ax.

Every operator satisfies its own characteristic equation χT(T)=0\chi_T(T)=0χT​(T)=0 (the Cayley–Hamilton theorem). With it we write the inverse matrix and high powers as low-degree polynomials. Spectral mapping sends an eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ to f(λ)f(\lambda)f(λ). So in quantum mechanics, once the Hamiltonian is diagonalized, we immediately have the time evolution e−iH^t/ℏe^{-i\hat Ht/\hbar}e−iH^t/ℏ.

  • Diagonalizable — has an eigenbasis   ⟺  \iff⟺ the eigenspace dimensions add up to dim⁡V\dim VdimV; dim⁡V\dim VdimV distinct eigenvalues suffice.
  • Diagonalization in practice — A=PDP−1A=PDP^{-1}A=PDP−1, so powers and functions are computed separately for each eigenvalue; etAe^{tA}etA solves x˙=Ax\dot x=Axx˙=Ax.
  • Cayley–Hamilton theorem — χT(T)=0\chi_T(T)=0χT​(T)=0; the inverse matrix and high powers are written as low-degree polynomials in TTT.
  • Spectral mapping — fff sends an eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ to f(λ)f(\lambda)f(λ); so diagonalizing HHH gives e−iHt/ℏe^{-iHt/\hbar}e−iHt/ℏ.
  • Jordan normal form — this form exists even when diagonalization fails (self-study).

Self-check

13 questions about what you have learned in this lecture. Think carefully before you answer — a wrong answer you thought about is worth more than a right one you guessed.

3 An operator T∈ℒ(V) is diagonalizable exactly when…

Here is the hint. Try once more — the explanation comes after that. What does a diagonal matrix say about each basis vector? That is the definition: in a basis of eigenvectors the matrix is diagonal, and conversely. dim V distinct eigenvalues suffice but are not needed (the identity has one eigenvalue). On a non-zero finite-dimensional complex space every operator has an eigenvalue and a triangular matrix, yet the shear is not diagonalizable.

4 An n×n matrix over 𝔽 has n distinct eigenvalues in 𝔽. It is…

Here is the hint. Try once more — the explanation comes after that. Count linearly independent eigenvectors. Distinct eigenvalues give n linearly independent eigenvectors, which is exactly a basis of eigenvectors. A zero eigenvalue changes nothing. The converse fails: a repeated eigenvalue may still diagonalize.

5 A=[[1,1],[0,1]] has the single eigenvalue 1. Which fact shows that A is not diagonalizable?

Here is the hint. Try once more — the explanation comes after that. Solve (A−I)v=0 and find the dimension of its solution set. The eigenvectors lie only along (1,0), so dim E(1,A)=1<2: one eigendirection cannot make a basis of ℝ², and no P diagonalizes A. det A=1 and tr A=2 are true, but the diagonalizable identity matrix I has the same determinant and trace.

6 Which matrix P gives P⁻¹AP=diag(3,−1) for A=[[1,2],[2,1]]?

Here is the hint. Try once more — the explanation comes after that. The columns of P are eigenvectors, in the same order as the eigenvalues on the diagonal of D. AP=PD says, column by column, that Avₖ=λₖvₖ. So the first column must be an eigenvector for 3 and the second one for −1: A(1,1)=(3,3)=3(1,1) and A(1,−1)=(−1,1)=−(1,−1), so P=[[1,1],[1,−1]]. Swapping the columns gives diag(−1,3). Neither A itself nor D=diag(3,−1) is built from eigenvectors.

7 A=PDP⁻¹ with D=diag(2,−1). What is tr A⁴?

A⁴=PD⁴P⁻¹, and similar matrices have the same trace.

Here is the hint. Try once more — the explanation comes after that. The middle factors cancel, so A⁴=PD⁴P⁻¹ with D⁴=diag(16,1). The trace does not change under similarity (Lecture 4), so tr A⁴=16+1=17, whatever P is.

8 A is 2×2 with tr A=3 and det A=2. Cayley–Hamilton gives A²=3A−cI. What is c?

For a 2×2 matrix the characteristic polynomial is λ²−(tr A)λ+det A.

Here is the hint. Try once more — the explanation comes after that. χ_A(λ)=λ²−3λ+2, so A²−3A+2I=0. Hence A²=3A−2I and c=2.

9 ẋ=Ax and Av=−2v. What is the solution with x(0)=v?

Here is the hint. Try once more — the explanation comes after that. The solution is x(t)=eᵗᴬv, and a function of A acts on an eigenvector through its eigenvalue. eᵗᴬv=e⁻²ᵗv, so the state stays on the eigendirection and decays exponentially.

10 T=2P₁−P₂ is a spectral decomposition: P₁P₂=P₂P₁=0 and P₁+P₂=I. What is T³?

Here is the hint. Try once more — the explanation comes after that. f(T)=f(λ₁)P₁+f(λ₂)P₂. Here f(λ)=λ³. T³=2³P₁+(−1)³P₂=8P₁−P₂. Multiplying out gives the same, because P₁²=P₁, P₂²=P₂ and the cross terms vanish.

11 T=diag(1,−1), so T²=I. Which statement is true?

Here is the hint. Try once more — the explanation comes after that. Spectral mapping takes eigenvectors of T to eigenvectors of f(T). Does it work backwards when f(1)=f(−1)? f(λ)=λ² sends both 1 and −1 to 1, so T²=I, and every non-zero vector is an eigenvector of I. But T(1,1)=(1,−1), so (1,1) is not an eigenvector of T: its eigendirections are only the two coordinate axes.

12 V≠{0} is a finite-dimensional complex vector space, and S,T∈ℒ(V) commute. What is guaranteed?

Here is the hint. Try once more — the explanation comes after that. An eigenspace E(λ,S) is invariant under T. T maps E(λ,S) into itself, so T has an eigenvector inside it, and that vector is an eigenvector of S too. A common basis also needs both operators to be diagonalizable: the identity commutes with the shear, which has no basis of eigenvectors. I and 2I commute but share no eigenvalue.

13 Self-study: in the Jordan form of a diagonalizable operator, every block has size…

Here is the hint. Try once more — the explanation comes after that. A block of size 2 or more contains a generalized eigenvector that is not an eigenvector. Diagonalizable means the Jordan form is already diagonal, which is exactly the statement that every block is 1×1.
